child_drafts.description_short: Trump removes NSA and Cyber Command chief Timothy Haugh after loyalty purge.
child_drafts.description_medium: On April 3, 2025, Gen. Timothy Haugh was removed as NSA director and Cyber Command chief, along with NSA deputy Wendy Noble. child_drafts.description_long: General Timothy Haugh was fired as director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command on April 3, 2025, and civilian NSA deputy Wendy Noble was also removed, The Washington Post reported. Haugh’s dismissal and Noble’s reassignment were confirmed by current and former officials who spoke anonymously. The Post reported that far-right activist Laura Loomer advocated for their removals in a meeting with President Trump the day before; Loomer later said she urged Trump to dismiss Haugh because of his association with retired General Mark Milley. Officials quoted by the Post said they were unaware of an official reason for the actions. The article identifies acting replacements and describes Haugh’s previous cyber-security service, but those details do not establish the administration’s motive. The event should be dated separately from the later revocation of security clearances for 37 intelligence officials. Reports of Loomer’s advocacy are relevant context, but the available source does not prove that it caused the firings.

child_drafts.description_long: On August 19, 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard announced that she had revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former government officials. A Washington Post report said Gabbard’s memorandum alleged that the targeted people had politicized intelligence, failed to protect classified information or fallen short of professional standards. The list included officials involved in a 2017 assessment of Russian election interference and people involved in investigations or impeachment proceedings during Trump’s first term. The Post separately reported that an unnamed senior CIA Russia specialist lost her clearance four days after the Alaska summit with Vladimir Putin, ending a 29-year public-service career and canceling an approved assignment in Europe. The article reports that the memo did not identify specific infractions for the analyst. Claims that the action was retaliation or a loyalty purge are interpretations attributed to former officials, not an established finding about motive. This August clearance action should not be merged with Haugh’s April dismissal.

child_drafts.title: Gabbard Fires National Intelligence Council Acting Chairman and Deputy (May 2025)
child_drafts.description_short: Gabbard Fires National Intelligence Council Acting Chairman and Deputy (May 2025).
child_drafts.description_medium: Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and deputy Maria Langan-Riekhof in May 2025, according to The Washington Post. The removals followed an assessment that contradicted the administration’s stated rationale for deportations; their direct role in drafting that assessment was unclear. The assessment was dated April 7 and was later partially declassified.
child_drafts.description_long: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard removed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and his deputy, Maria Langan-Riekhof, in May 2025, The Washington Post reported. Their departures came about a week after the council produced a partially declassified assessment stating that Venezuela’s government was most likely not directing the Tren de Aragua gang’s activity in the United States. That assessment undercut a rationale the Trump administration had used for invoking the Alien Enemies Act to deport alleged gang members. The Post said it was unclear whether Collins or Langan-Riekhof had a direct role in preparing the assessment, which was attributed to a National Intelligence Officer for the Western Hemisphere. The intelligence office spokesperson said Gabbard was working with Trump to end politicization of the intelligence community; lawmakers criticized the removals and warned they could chill independent analysis. The event should be stated as personnel removals following the report, while avoiding a definitive causal claim absent documentation.

child_drafts.description_short: Reuters reported the CIA fired more than a few probationary recent hires in early March 2025; the agency did not disclose a count.
child_drafts.description_medium: In early March 2025, the CIA fired an unspecified number of probationary recent hires, Reuters reported. The agency said it was reviewing employees in their first two years; an unnamed source said congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when dismissals began. Reuters said the dismissals began earlier that week and affected more than a few hires.
child_drafts.description_long: The CIA terminated a number of recent hires in early March 2025 as part of a review of probationary employees, Reuters reported. Three people familiar with the matter said the dismissals affected more than a few employees, but the agency did not disclose a total. A CIA spokesperson said the agency was reviewing personnel in their first two years of service and that some reviews would result in termination. The employees worked across several portfolios, and a person familiar with the matter cited performance issues as the stated basis for some terminations. Reuters also reported, based on an unnamed source, that congressional intelligence committees had not been informed when the dismissals began, despite such notification being customary. The agency’s announcement supports a discrete staffing action, but the article does not verify a specific number or that all probationary officers were fired. The held language “mass firing” overstates the public evidence; claims about required notification and national-security effects should be attributed to the cited source or experts.

child_drafts.description_long: The Washington Post reported that Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard’s August 19, 2025 memorandum revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former officials. The memo cited alleged politicization of intelligence, failures to protect classified material or departures from professional standards, but did not identify specific infractions for every person named. Four days after the Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, an unnamed senior CIA Russia analyst was ordered to surrender her clearance, according to the Post. She had served in public intelligence work for 29 years and had an approved assignment in Europe; the clearance action ended that career. The Post reported that she had helped prepare the administration for the summit, but the report does not establish that the summit itself caused the revocation. This is the same August clearance action proposed in entry 5224’s second child. The two cards should be linked as duplicate coverage of one event, with a single event record describing the wider list and the separately reported CIA analyst impact.
